+# Run Causal Conv1d operators
+
+Use `cudnn.ops` Causal Conv1d operators when their fixed CUDA layouts and fused autograd registrations match the model. Use Graph convolution for general N-D padding, dilation, or layout requirements.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+You need CUDA-enabled PyTorch and a package built with the optional causal
+convolution bindings. Check `hasattr(cudnn, "causal_conv1d_forward")` before
+registering this path. Use the [convolution tutorial](/tutorials/convolution)
+when the optional binding is absent or its fixed layouts do not fit the model.
+
+## causal_conv1d
+
+`cudnn.ops.causal_conv1d(x, weight, bias=None, activation="identity")` computes depthwise causal convolution with `K - 1` zeros on the left and no right padding.
+
+| Value | Shape | Requirements |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `x` | `[batch, channels, sequence]` | CUDA, FP32/FP16/BF16; copied if noncontiguous |
+| `weight` | `[channels, kernel_size]` | Same device and dtype as X |
+| `bias` | `[channels]` | Optional; same device and dtype; zeros when omitted |
+| result | `[batch, channels, sequence]` | Same dtype and device as X |
+
+`activation` is `"identity"` or `"silu"`. Each channel has an independent filter. The registered backward returns gradients for X, weight, and bias; the wrapper participates in eager autograd, fake-tensor propagation, and `torch.compile`.
+
+## causal_conv1d_nwh
+
+`cudnn.ops.causal_conv1d_nwh(x, weight, bias=None, activation="identity")` performs the same operation in NWH storage:
+
+| Value | Shape |
+| --- | --- |
+| `x` | `[batch, sequence, channels]` |
+| `weight` | `[kernel_size, channels]` |
+| `bias` | `[channels]` |
+| result | `[batch, sequence, channels]` |
+
+The device, dtype, activation, fake-tensor, autograd, and compilation rules are the same as for `causal_conv1d`. The two wrappers are layout-specific. They call `.contiguous()` before the raw binding, so a transposed view is accepted but may allocate and copy; use the native layout when that cost matters.
+
+## b2b_causal_conv1d
+
+`cudnn.ops.b2b_causal_conv1d(x, weights_proj, weights_mixer, skip_bias)` fuses a projection convolution, Q/K gate, mixer convolution with a skip term, and final V gate.
+
+| Value | Shape |
+| --- | --- |
+| `x` | `[batch, 3 * channels, sequence]` |
+| `weights_proj` | `[3 * channels, projection_kernel]` |
+| `weights_mixer` | `[channels, mixer_kernel]` |
+| `skip_bias` | `[channels]` |
+| result | `[batch, channels, sequence]` |
+
+All tensors must be CUDA tensors on one device with one dtype. The channel extent of X must be divisible by three. Backward computes gradients for all four inputs using the saved projected intermediate.
+
+## Low-level pointer bindings
+
+When the compiled extension was built with the optional kernels, top-level functions named `causal_conv1d_forward`, `causal_conv1d_backward`, `causal_conv1d_nwh_forward`, `causal_conv1d_nwh_backward`, `b2b_causal_conv1d_forward`, and `b2b_causal_conv1d_backward` accept a CUDA stream, raw device pointers, dimensions, dtype codes, and operation-specific options. Test availability with `hasattr(cudnn, "causal_conv1d_forward")` before registering a production path.
+
+These bindings do not validate PyTorch ownership, allocate outputs, register fake behavior, or connect autograd. Use them only when the application already owns buffer lifetime and stream ordering. Keep every pointer alive until the supplied stream completes.
+
+## Test eager, backward, and compile paths
+
+The canonical sample runs the high-level channel-first operator, checks forward values and gradients against PyTorch convolution, then executes a compiled wrapper:
+
+<Code
+  src="../samples/python/causal_conv1d.py"
+  language="python"
+  maxLines={0}
+/>
+
+Current source: [PyTorch operators and registrations](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/0a07d4ee28f8ae2f2106bb766b1878cc732ee80c/python/cudnn/ops/causal_conv1d.py#L35).
+
+## Verification limits
+
+The recorded Python extension did not export `causal_conv1d_forward` or the
+other five optional bindings, so the high-level operator raised `AttributeError`
+before launch. The wrapper delegates architecture checks to those compiled
+bindings and does not expose a separate support query. The raw-pointer
+functions also do not have individual API pages.
+
+## Expected result
+
+When the optional bindings are present, the Python sample checks eager output
+and gradients against PyTorch and runs the operator through `torch.compile`.
+There is no C++ counterpart because this guide covers a PyTorch dispatcher
+operator; use C++ Graph convolution for a language-neutral implementation.

+# Capture and update a CUDA Graph
+
+Populate cuDNN work into a CUDA Graph, instantiate it, replay it with stable resources, and update supported bindings without rebuilding the frontend graph.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Start with a built C++ graph and a supported CUDA Graph runtime. Keep all
+captured allocations alive, bind the intended stream to the cuDNN handle, and

+Python Graph wrapper does not expose this lifecycle.

+## Populate and instantiate

+## Update bindings
+
+Use `update_cuda_graph` only for the updates documented by the backend. Stable-address requirements still apply to resources captured by address. When shapes, plan, node topology, or unsupported bindings change, repopulate and reinstantiate instead.

+instantiated and replayed with stable resources; documented binding updates

+# Inspect automatic Python engine selection
+
+`cudnn.pygraph` ranks the Python engines shipped in the library together with cuDNN backend plans. Applications select among the resulting plans; they do not register engines or replace the routing policy at runtime.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Use the explicit `cudnn.pygraph` lifecycle and construct a graph that is supported by the installed cuDNN release. Python-engine routing remains an unreleased interface, so do not persist plan indices across frontend versions.
+
+## Inspect the graph
+
+Graph inspection is available before planning:
+
+<Markdown src="/snippets/generated/python/custom_engine/inspection.mdx" />
+
+Use named ports, tensor metadata, and `NodeType` when diagnosing engine support. Insertion order is not an execution contract.
+
+## Inspect automatic selection
+
+<Markdown src="/snippets/generated/python/custom_engine/routing.mdx" />
+
+`create_execution_plans()` discovers candidate Python engines from the in-tree manifest and queries the backend for the requested heuristic modes. Mode B asks the backend for a broader search; Python engine families use their mode-A recommendations because they do not expose a separate mode-B candidate set. `graph.plans` contains the combined ranked list.
+
+`graph.selected_engine` identifies an in-tree Python engine. A value of `None` means the selected entry is owned by the cuDNN backend. `select_plan()` pins an index strictly: if that entry cannot build, the call fails instead of silently moving to another plan.
+
+## Execute the selected plan
+
+<Markdown src="/snippets/generated/python/custom_engine/execution.mdx" />
+
+The caller owns tensor buffers, workspace, handles, and stream lifetime. The selected implementation must preserve the graph's declared output and asynchronous execution contract.
+
+## Add an engine to the library
+
+Library contributors add an engine to `python/cudnn/engines/manifest.py`, give it a stable family slot, implement exact support and build contracts, and add family-level analyzer and heuristic hooks when ranking requires them. Runtime engine registration is intentionally unsupported: a caller-provided engine would not have a manifest capability record or a stable plan identity.
+
+See [Python IR routing invariants](/concepts/python-ir-routing) for the dispatch model. The retained Fern source contains the complete contributor contract in `docs/utilities/python_graph_and_execution_backends.md`.
+
+## Expected result
+
+The sample prints whether the first ranked plan belongs to an in-tree Python engine or the cuDNN backend, executes that plan, and checks its result against PyTorch.

+# Serialize, precompile, and deploy graphs
+
+Prepare graphs on one system and load them in another only when the serialization format and target properties are compatible.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Begin with a graph that already builds and passes numerical checks. Record the
+frontend, backend, CUDA, and target-device versions before treating serialized
+bytes as a deployable artifact.
+
+## Choose a representation
+
+`serialize()` preserves the cuDNN backend graph representation. Create a compatible `pygraph`, then call its `deserialize()` method to reconstruct that representation. Python engine objects and arbitrary inspection dictionaries are not part of the format.
+
+<Code
+  src="../samples/python/serialize_basic.py"
+  language="python"
+  maxLines={0}
+/>
+
+## Record target properties
+
+Capture frontend and backend versions, CUDA runtime, GPU architecture, device properties, graph key, operation attributes, and build policy. Structure-free or deviceless ahead-of-time compilation must receive explicit target SM and device properties instead of reading the current device implicitly.
+
+## Run the three-stage deviceless flow
+
+1. On a representative target device, construct `DeviceProperties`, initialize it with `set_device_id(device)` or `set_handle(handle)`, call `build()`, and serialize the descriptor. This stage requires the device.
+2. On the build host, deserialize those bytes into a new `DeviceProperties`, attach it with `graph.set_device_properties(...)`, describe the graph, build a plan with the no-handle lifecycle, and serialize the graph or plan. This stage is intended to run without the target device.
+3. On a device with matching properties, deserialize with a live cuDNN handle, query workspace, bind variant-pack pointers, and execute. Reject a property mismatch instead of assuming that the serialized plan will re-specialize.
+
+Device-property bytes and graph bytes are separate artifacts. Version them together with the target commit, cuDNN backend version, build policy, and operation metadata. A serialized `DeviceProperties` object describes the target; it does not prove that every operation has a deviceless heuristic or compiler path.
+
+## Control warmup
+
+Use warmup to materialize lazy kernels or caches before latency-sensitive service. Bind representative, valid buffers and workspace. Warmup does not replace correctness testing and may not cover every dynamic specialization.
+
+## Validate on load
+
+Reject incompatible metadata before execution. Rebuild when serialization or device compatibility cannot be established. Keep a source-graph path available for cache misses and deployment upgrades.
+
+References: [`serialize`](/api/python/serialize), [`deserialize`](/api/python/deserialize), [`warmup`](/api/cpp/warmup), and [`set_device_properties`](/api/cpp/set-device-properties).
+
+## Verification limits
+
+The recorded sample verified serialization in one process on a single-GPU
+host. Cross-process artifact transfer and a genuinely deviceless build stage
+were not exercised, so that run does not establish deployment isolation.
+
+## Expected result
+
+The serialization sample round-trips a graph and executes it on a compatible
+target. Production loading must reject incompatible metadata and fall back to
+rebuilding; the published verification does not establish a cross-process or
+genuinely deviceless deployment.

+# Run dynamic shapes with a kernel cache
+
+Build a graph that accepts documented shape or stride overrides and attach a kernel cache so compatible specializations can be reused.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Use C++ with cuDNN 9.23 or newer for the override-aware workspace query. Start
+from a graph that passes at fixed shapes and choose explicit minimum, maximum,
+and incompatible cases for every dimension you intend to vary.
+
+## Enable the mode
+
+Set dynamic-shape or override-shape mode before validation. They are graph construction properties and cannot be enabled after creating the graph representation or after planning freezes the graph.
+
+## Identify overridden tensors
+
+Supply corresponding arrays of UIDs, shapes, and strides at execution. Each UID must belong to the graph, each shape must have the expected rank, and each stride must describe the supplied storage. Omitted tensors retain compiled metadata.
+
+The three arrays must have identical lengths and matching positions. Override every materialized tensor whose metadata changes, including outputs and auxiliary statistics. A changed input shape does not implicitly rewrite the output shape or stride supplied to the backend.
+
+## Query runtime workspace before allocation
+
+For every override set, call the overload of `get_workspace_size(handle, ..., override_uids, override_shapes, override_strides)` before allocating workspace. Then execute with the same three arrays. Runtime specialization can require more or less workspace than the cache shape used to build the graph, so a buffer sized only from parameterless `get_workspace_size()` is not a general bound.
+
+The C++ override workspace query requires cuDNN 9.23 in the current implementation. On older backends, do not assume the build-shape query is sufficient for arbitrary runtime shapes. Either restrict overrides to a separately established bound, rebuild per shape, or upgrade before deploying an unbounded override workflow.
+
+Allocate one workspace per overlapping execution or use a stream-aware pool. Querying the right byte count does not make one mutable buffer safe for concurrent streams.
+
+## Attach a kernel cache
+
+Create a cache with `cudnn.create_kernel_cache()` or the C++ `KernelCache`, attach it before build, and keep it alive while graphs use it. Serialized cache data is backend- and compatibility-sensitive; validate device and backend properties before reuse.
+
+## Bound specialization
+
+Dynamic support is operation and engine specific. Test minimum, maximum, boundary, and incompatible shapes. A successful override on one plan does not establish support for every candidate.
+
+Relevant references: [`set_dynamic_shape_enabled`](/api/cpp/set-dynamic-shape-enabled), [`set_override_shape_enabled`](/api/cpp/set-override-shape-enabled), and [`set_kernel_cache`](/api/cpp/set-kernel-cache).
+
+## Verification limits
+
+No documentation-owned dynamic-shape execution sample is published. The
+recorded cuDNN 9.15.1 backend is below the 9.23 gate for the override-aware
+workspace query, so the ordering contract was verified from source rather than
+by runtime execution.
+
+## Expected result
+
+For every accepted override, the runtime workspace query and execution use the
+same UID, shape, and stride arrays, and compatible specializations reuse the
+attached cache. This repository does not publish a runtime example, so those
+properties must be established on the deployment backend.

+# Control the explicit `cudnn.pygraph` lifecycle
+
+Use the explicit lifecycle when you need to inspect graph state, filter backend plans, route to Python engines, serialize, or control runtime buffers yourself.
+
+Python IR routing, its routed/backend index spaces, and its one-shot planning
+contract are unreleased in this checkout. See
+[Python IR routing availability](/concepts/python-ir-routing#availability).
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Complete [Build and extend a graph](/tutorials/first-graph) first. Use
+`cudnn.pygraph` here only when the high-level context manager does not expose
+the plan inspection, routing, serialization, or buffer control you need.
+
+## Build in stages
+
+The stages follow one ordered path:
+
+1. `graph.validate()` checks Python IR and infers properties; the backend path may create the graph representation here so unsupported graphs can fail early.
+2. `graph.build_operation_graph()` finalizes backend operation descriptors and makes backend engine queries available.
+3. `graph.create_execution_plans()` builds one ranked list from eligible in-tree Python engines and the backend candidates returned for the requested heuristic modes.
+4. `graph.select_plan()` chooses an entry from that combined list. Backend at-index methods operate in a separate index space.
+5. `graph.check_support()` lets the selected engine reject the graph before compilation.
+6. `graph.build_plans()` compiles the selected entry once. Planning and graph mutation are one-shot; construct a new graph to re-plan.
+7. `graph.get_workspace_size()` determines required temporary storage.
+8. `graph.execute()` binds every non-virtual tensor and enqueues work on the handle stream.
+
+The [engine-selection sample](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/main/docs/samples/python/custom_engine.py) exercises routed
+planning. The [`graph.execute()` sample](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/main/docs/samples/python/execute_basic.py)
+uses the explicit backend lifecycle, binds runtime buffers, and executes a
+matmul. The higher-level [matmul sample](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/main/docs/samples/python/matmul_basic.py) is a
+contrast: `cudnn.Graph` performs the build stages inside its wrapper.
+

+# Build and cache with `cudnn.graph`, `cudnn.jit`, and `graph_cache`
+
+Use the decorators in `cudnn.graph` to construct a `cudnn.Graph` lazily from PyTorch calls and cache it by the metadata that controls graph compatibility.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+You need CUDA-enabled PyTorch and a cuDNN Graph backend supported by the
+decorator. Complete [Build and extend a graph](/tutorials/first-graph) and
+identify every piece of metadata that changes the graph contract.
+
+## Choose the decorator
+
+- `@cudnn.graph(...)` wraps one function and uses the default graph cache unless another cache is supplied.
+- `@cudnn.jit(...)` accepts the same graph-building options and is the concise JIT-style spelling.
+- `cudnn.graph_cache(key_fn, maxsize=256)` creates a bounded cache decorator with a caller-defined key.
+
+## Define a complete key
+
+Include device identity, dtype, shape, stride, training mode, scalar attributes, and any option that changes the graph. The built-in default key covers positional tensor metadata and keyword values but application containers or hidden global state may require an explicit `key_fn`.
+
+## Handle eviction and failures
+
+The cache is least-recently-used through `functools.lru_cache`. Eviction releases the Python wrapper when no other references remain. A failed graph build is not a valid cache result; correct the metadata or support condition rather than reusing a partially built wrapper.
+
+Source contracts: [`python/cudnn/graph.py`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/0a07d4ee28f8ae2f2106bb766b1878cc732ee80c/python/cudnn/graph.py#L1).
+
+The complete cache examples are available in
+[Python](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/main/docs/samples/python/pytorch_cached_graph.py) and
+[C++](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/main/docs/samples/cpp/graph_cache.cc).
+
+## Expected result
+
+Both examples build one graph entry, execute it with two compatible sets of
+buffers, and compare the results with an independent calculation. A changed
+shape, stride, dtype, device, or behavior-controlling option produces a
+different cache entry.

+# Migrate from the legacy C++ builder API
+
+Move descriptor-by-descriptor code to the modern Graph API while preserving layouts, operation attributes, engine policy, and runtime bindings.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Inventory one legacy graph and capture its dimensions, strides, UIDs, data
+types, attributes, selected-plan policy, workspace, output values, and error
+behavior. Keep that result as the migration baseline.
+
+## Map the construction model
+
+| Legacy builder | Modern Graph API |
+| --- | --- |
+| Tensor, convolution, pointwise, reduction descriptors | `Tensor_attributes` and operation-specific attribute values |
+| Operation builders and `OperationGraph` | Calls on `cudnn_frontend::graph::Graph` |
+| Engine heuristics/config generators | Graph heuristic and plan-creation methods |
+| `ExecutionPlan` | Built Graph plan or at-index plan |
+| `VariantPack` | Tensor-attribute-to-pointer map plus workspace |
+| Exception/status builder checks | `error_t` checks at each Graph lifecycle stage |
+
+## Migrate one graph at a time
+
+Record the old graph's tensor dimensions, strides, UIDs, types, operation attributes, notes, workspace, and numerical results. Rebuild the same graph with modern attributes, compare output and resource behavior, then replace plan-selection code. Do not mix legacy and modern descriptor ownership unless a documented interoperability API permits it.
+
+## Keep legacy reference scoped
+
+Legacy headers remain installed for compatibility, but new examples and tutorials should use the Graph API. Mark behavior that exists only in a legacy descriptor rather than implying a modern equivalent.
+
+## Expected result
+
+The modern Graph produces the same numerical result and compatible resource
+behavior as the recorded legacy graph. Migrate and verify one complete graph at
+a time, then remove its legacy construction and execution path.

+# Advanced: convert graphs to FP8, MXFP8, or NVFP4
+
+Introduce low precision as an explicit quantize, scale, compute, and validate pipeline rather than only changing an enum.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Establish a BF16 or FP32 baseline first. Check the required GPU architecture,
+cuDNN and CUDA versions, scale layout, and dimension multiples for the format;
+then complete the [block-scaling tutorial](/tutorials/block-scaling) for
+MXFP8 or NVFP4 work.
+
+## Choose the format
+
+FP8 is available on Hopper and later for supported operations. MXFP8 and NVFP4 use block scaling and target Blackwell paths in this checkout. Each path defines scale granularity, packed layout, reorder type, dimension multiples, and output/amax behavior.
+
+## Build the dataflow
+
+1. Compute or receive an amax value in a supported precision.
+2. Derive scale and reciprocal scale using the documented block granularity.
+3. Quantize and reorder values into the operation's required representation.
+4. Bind scale or descale tensors as runtime data.
+5. Execute with a supported compute type and materialize output/amax state.
+6. Dequantize or compare in higher precision.
+
+The [Python block-scaled matmul sample](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/main/docs/samples/python/block_scaled_matmul.py)
+and its [C++ counterpart](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/main/docs/samples/cpp/block_scaled_matmul.cc) execute an
+MXFP8 dequantize, matmul, and block-scale quantize graph. Use them as the
+starting point for checking scale layout and output metadata.
+
+## Validate accuracy and support
+
+Measure saturation, underflow, relative error, and task-level tolerance. Keep a BF16 or FP32 reference. Record the exact SM, cuDNN, CUDA, shapes, layout, and format because support is not interchangeable across low-precision names.
+
+## Verification limits
+
+Python and C++ MXFP8 block-scaled matmul samples and C++ FP8 and MXFP8
+attention samples executed on SM100. An NVFP4 end-to-end path and a standalone
+block-scale round trip were not verified.
+
+## Expected result
+
+The selected low-precision path remains within the application's measured
+error and saturation limits and passes on every deployed architecture. The
+published block-scaled matmul and C++ attention samples establish their
+specific MXFP8 and FP8 paths on SM100; they do not establish NVFP4 or
+arbitrary-operation support.

+# Configure matmul layouts and projections
+
+Describe matrix multiplication with logical dimensions and explicit strides. The final two dimensions are `M x K` for `A` and `K x N` for `B`; leading dimensions are broadcast-compatible batches.

+# Choose a normalization family
+
+Select a family from the axes it reduces, the state it maintains, and the statistics its backward path needs.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Complete the [normalization tutorial](/tutorials/normalization). Identify
+the axes to reduce, whether running state changes, and which saved statistics
+the backward graph consumes before choosing a family.
+
+| Family | Typical reduction | State and outputs |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| BatchNorm | Batch and spatial dimensions per channel | Saved mean/inverse variance; optional running mean/variance |
+| BatchNorm inference | Uses established channel statistics | No training update |
+| LayerNorm | One or more trailing feature dimensions | Saved mean/inverse variance for backward |
+| RMSNorm | Trailing feature dimensions without mean subtraction | Saved inverse variance for backward |
+| InstanceNorm | Spatial dimensions per sample and channel | Saved statistics for backward |
+| Adaptive LayerNorm | LayerNorm plus learned conditioning | Family-specific scale/bias outputs and gradients |
+
+## Configure training
+
+Use `norm_forward_phase.TRAINING` where the API exposes it. Materialize saved statistics when backward runs in a separate graph. Keep epsilon's lifetime valid as a pass-by-value or supported graph tensor. Bind running-state outputs if the family updates them.
+
+## Use generated statistics
+
+`genstats` returns sum and squared sum. `bn_finalize` combines statistics with scale, bias, epsilon, accumulation count, and optional running state. Do not substitute one family's statistics layout for another.
+
+Canonical examples: [LayerNorm forward](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/main/docs/samples/python/layernorm_basic.py) and [LayerNorm backward](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/main/docs/samples/python/layernorm_backward_basic.py). The BatchNorm API page records the missing standalone-sample gap.

+[C++ backward](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/main/docs/samples/cpp/layernorm_backward_basic.cc).

+The selected family produces the expected normalized output and saved state.

+# Select, filter, and autotune plans
+
+Create candidate plans, remove configurations that violate application requirements, and benchmark the remaining plans with representative buffers.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Complete the [explicit lifecycle](/how-to/explicit-lifecycle) with a graph that has
+more than one supported candidate. Define workspace, determinism, numerical,
+and latency policy before filtering or timing candidates.
+
+## Keep index spaces separate
+
+Python `graph.plans` is the combined list of eligible in-tree Python plans and cuDNN backend candidates. `select_plan()` chooses from that list. Backend methods such as `build_plan_at_index()` use the backend's separate plan index space.
+
+## Filter backend candidates
+
+After `build_operation_graph()`, use engine, behavior-note, numerical-note, workspace, and shared-memory filters. A filter changes the eligible set; it does not prove numerical acceptability. Keep determinism, down-conversion, and reduced-precision notes aligned with application policy.
+
+## Autotune
+
+Allocate the maximum required workspace for candidates, warm up each plan, time multiple executions on the intended stream, synchronize at measurement boundaries, and choose a stable statistic. Use representative shapes and pointer alignment. Re-run when the backend, driver, GPU, or graph metadata changes.
+
+<Markdown src="/snippets/generated/cpp/plan_inspection/autotune.mdx" />
+
+## Control compilation
+
+Build one selected plan or use the documented parallel build policy. SM carveout and engine knobs can change support and resource requirements. Persist a choice only with a compatibility key that includes the graph and target environment.
+
+References: [`create_execution_plans`](/api/python/create-execution-plans), [`deselect_workspace_greater_than`](/api/cpp/deselect-workspace-greater-than), and [`autotune`](/api/cpp/autotune).

+executable example for Python routed-plan index mapping is not yet published.

+
+Use `cudnn.Graph` when PyTorch owns runtime tensors and you want the frontend to automate lifecycle stages, output allocation, workspace, handle reuse, and current-stream binding.
+
+`cudnn.Graph` requires cuDNN backend 9.12 or newer. The repository's general
+frontend minimum of 8.5 does not apply to this wrapper; see
+[installation requirements](/getting-started/installation#verification-limits).
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Install CUDA-enabled PyTorch and cuDNN backend 9.12 or newer, then complete
+[Build and extend a graph](/tutorials/first-graph). Use this wrapper when
+PyTorch tensors should define and supply the graph contract.
+
+## Declare the call contract
+
+Pass `inputs` and `outputs` as ordered names, graph tensors, or representative PyTorch tensors. Names must resolve to tensors captured during construction. Positional calls bind in that declared order; dictionary-oriented execution uses tensor names or descriptors through the underlying graph.
+
+<Code
+  src="../samples/python/matmul.py"
+  language="python"
+  maxLines={0}
+/>
+
+## Build on context exit
+
+Inside the context, operation methods are forwarded to an owned `cudnn.pygraph`. On successful exit the wrapper validates, creates the graph representation, queries heuristic plans, checks support, builds, allocates workspace when enabled, and resolves the IO tuples. An exception discards the incomplete graph.
+
+## Control resources
+
+`handle="auto"` uses a cached handle and updates its CUDA stream to PyTorch's current stream at execution. Supply a handle when the application owns it. Set `workspace_alloc=False` only when you will provide a compatible workspace through a lower-level path; the wrapper cannot execute without enough storage.
+
+## Reuse safely
+
+Reuse the wrapper with buffers whose shape, stride, dtype, and device satisfy the built graph. Build a distinct cache entry for a new metadata signature. `set_io_tuples()` can change the ordered wrapper contract before execution but cannot make incompatible tensor metadata legal.

+See [`cudnn.Graph`](/api/python#g) and [Your first graph](/tutorials/first-graph).

+use the [C++ quick start](/getting-started/quickstart).

+## Expected result
+
+The sample builds a matrix-multiplication graph on context exit, executes it
+with PyTorch tensors, and matches `torch.matmul`. Reusing the wrapper with

+distinct graph or cache entry.

+

+## Before you begin

+[Build and extend a graph](/tutorials/first-graph), and define the public
+operator schema plus every input property that changes graph compatibility.
+
+## Define the schema
+
+Use `torch.library.custom_op` or the lower-level `torch.library.Library.define/impl` API to declare tensor, scalar, optional, list, mutation, and aliasing behavior precisely. The current repository uses both styles. Choose one registration owner for a qualified operator name and keep its defaults consistent with the public Python wrapper.
+
+The canonical sample uses `custom_op` because it provides concise fake and autograd registration on the installed PyTorch version:
+
+<Markdown src="/snippets/generated/python/pytorch_custom_operator/registration.mdx" />
+
+Do not assume that `custom_op` adds a fixed amount of dispatch overhead. The current source uses it for Causal Conv1d; benchmark the chosen registration form with the deployed PyTorch version.
+
+## Register CUDA and fake implementations
+
+The CUDA kernel builds or retrieves a metadata-keyed cuDNN graph and executes it on the current stream. The fake implementation computes only output shapes, strides, dtypes, devices, and aliasing. It must not allocate CUDA storage or call cuDNN.
+
+Include device, dtype, shape, stride, and every scalar or enum that changes graph structure in the cache key. A shape-only key can incorrectly reuse a plan for a transposed or differently aligned tensor. The sample builds one `cudnn.Graph` per complete input metadata key:
+
+<Markdown src="/snippets/generated/python/pytorch_custom_operator/cache.mdx" />

+For explicit `cudnn.pygraph` integrations, derive the UID order once with `_get_variant_pack_uids_sorted()` only when using that internal fast path, build pointers in exactly that order, and call `_execute_with_ptrs`. Those underscore methods are not stable public APIs. Prefer the public `execute` or `cudnn.Graph.__call__` path unless measured Python overhead requires the internal path.
+
+Allocate workspace per concurrent execution. Caching the required byte count is safe for one compiled metadata signature; caching one mutable workspace tensor is not safe when streams can overlap. A `cudnn.Graph` wrapper manages workspace internally, while explicit `pygraph` code should allocate or pool storage with stream-aware ownership.

+When using explicit handles, cache at most one handle per device and call `cudnn.set_stream(handle, torch.cuda.current_stream(device).cuda_stream)` before every launch whose stream may differ. The wrapper's `handle="auto"` path performs current-stream binding for the sample.

+
+Save exactly the forward tensors and statistics needed by backward. Return gradients in schema order and `None` for non-differentiable arguments. Test repeated backward, non-contiguous layouts, and mixed requires-grad inputs.

+
+Configure pooling or resampling windows with explicit window dimensions, strides, pre-padding, post-padding, and padding mode.

When `0 < rope_dim < head_dim`, the operation rotates the last `rope_dim` features and applies scaled pass-through to the leading `head_dim - rope_dim` features. The frequency tensor's last dimension must equal `rope_dim`; `rope_dim=0` selects full-head rotation. Apply any output scaling explicitly and keep the frequency tensor dtype compatible with the chosen compute path.
+
+## Build backward
+
+<Tabs>
+<Tab title="Python" language="python">
+
+

+  language="python"

+Backward consumes the upstream gradient and the same frequency representation as forward. Preserve the same pairing and partial-dimension convention.
+
+## Integrate with attention
+
+Rotate query and key before SDPA, or use an attention option that explicitly accepts RoPE metadata. Do not apply both paths to the same tensor. For YaRN frequency helpers, record base, scaling factor, original maximum position, and dtype in the graph cache key.
+
+## Fold attention scale into RoPE
+
+SDPA normally forms scores as `alpha * Q_rotated * K_rotated^T`, where `alpha` is usually `1 / sqrt(D)`. The RoPE `output_scale` multiplies both rotated pairs and the pass-through portion of the output. You may therefore move the scale into either RoPE input to SDPA:
+
+- Q-only: set Q RoPE `output_scale=alpha`, K RoPE `output_scale=1`, and SDPA `attn_scale=1`.
+- K-only: set Q RoPE `output_scale=1`, K RoPE `output_scale=alpha`, and SDPA `attn_scale=1`.
+- Symmetric: choose scales whose product is alpha, commonly `sqrt(alpha)` for both, and set SDPA `attn_scale=1`.
+
+Backward must follow the same factorization. Pass the matching forward scale to each `rope_backward` operation and use the same SDPA backward attention scale as forward. Moving alpha changes where the chain-rule factor is applied; omitting it or applying it twice produces incorrect Q and K gradients even when forward scores appear plausible.
+
+YaRN returns an `mscale` intended for RoPE `output_scale`. When combining YaRN magnitude scaling with attention scaling, multiply the intended factors according to the chosen Q-only, K-only, or symmetric factorization and include them in graph cache identity.
+
+The current public SDPA API does not expose an `input_is_log2` option. Do not assume that a softmax base-conversion optimization is available through this interface.
+
+## Verification limits
+
+The public `cudnn.yarn` helpers do not have individual API pages or executable
+documentation samples. RoPE scale folding is source-backed, but the published
+samples do not compare folded and unfurled forward and gradient results.
+
+## Expected result

+On cuDNN 9.24 or newer, the paired forward and backward samples execute with
+matching layouts and frequency tensors and compare their outputs with
+independent RoPE calculations. In the recorded cuDNN 9.15.1 environment, the
+C++ samples compiled and the Python samples passed syntax checks only.
+Scale-folding equivalence and public YaRN helpers remain outside the published
+runtime verification and need separate forward and gradient checks.

+# Manage handles, streams, workspace, and variant packs
+
+Keep graph metadata reusable while making runtime ownership explicit.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Start with a built graph that already passes a numerical check. Decide which
+component owns the cuDNN handle, CUDA stream, workspace, runtime tensors, and
+pass-by-value storage for the full asynchronous execution lifetime.
+
+## Own the handle
+
+A cuDNN handle carries the CUDA stream and backend context. In Python, create and destroy it with `cudnn.create_handle()` and `destroy_handle()`, or let `cudnn.Graph(handle="auto")` manage a cached handle. In C++, use `cudnnCreate` and `cudnnDestroy` with RAII in application code.
+
+## Bind the stream
+
+Set or query the stream with `cudnn.set_stream()` and `get_stream()`, or `cudnnSetStream` and `cudnnGetStream`. Execution is asynchronous. Keep inputs, outputs, pass-by-value storage, workspace, graph, plan, and handle valid until dependent work completes.
+
+## Allocate workspace
+
+Call `get_workspace_size()` after the selected plan is built. Allocate at least that many device bytes with suitable alignment. Reuse workspace only when concurrent executions cannot overlap on the same storage.
+
+## Build the variant pack
+
+Bind each non-virtual tensor UID to a compatible device pointer. C++ maps `shared_ptr<Tensor_attributes>` to pointers; Python accepts tensor objects, UIDs, or supported names and extracts pointers from integers, PyTorch tensors, or DLPack providers. Use sorted UID/template helpers only with the graph and plan that produced them.
+
+The [C++ quick start](/getting-started/quickstart) uses `cudaMallocManaged()` for inspectable data and a separate device workspace.
+
+## Expected result
+
+Repeated executions use the intended stream, bind every non-virtual tensor,
+and keep all pointers and workspace valid until work completes. Concurrent
+executions use nonoverlapping workspace unless the allocator provides an
+equivalent stream-safe ownership guarantee.

+# Use scalar, pass-by-value, and compile-time constant tensors
+
+Choose a scalar representation from when the value is known and where its storage lives.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Use the C++ Graph API for the complete compile-time-constant example. Decide
+whether the value belongs to graph identity, changes between executions, or is
+ordinary device data before choosing its representation.
+
+## Pass by value
+
+`tensor_scalar` and scalar `Tensor_attributes` create scalar-shaped graph values. Pass-by-value values are bound from host-visible storage according to the backend variant-pack contract; keep that storage valid until the asynchronous operation has consumed it.
+
+## Compile-time constants
+
+C++ scalar constructors with `ScalarType::COMPILE_TIME_CONST` embed supported values into graph construction. Changing the value changes the graph and can require a new plan. Use only supported scalar types and include the value in serialization and cache identity.
+
+The C++ Graph has compile-time scalar overloads for `float`, `double`, `half`, `bfloat16`, `int32_t`, and `int64_t`. The Python binding exposes `float`, `double`, `int32_t`, and `int64_t` overloads through `tensor_scalar(value, cudnn.scalar_type.COMPILE_TIME_CONST)`; Python numeric conversion and pybind overload resolution determine the selected C++ type.
+
+Under the hood, `Tensor_attributes::set_compile_time_constant(...)` stores the payload and `get_has_compile_time_constant()` reports it. A compile-time constant must be pass-by-value and non-virtual. It must not also carry a runtime `pass_by_value` payload. Prefer `tensor_scalar` over manipulating those flags directly because the scalar constructor establishes the invariant as one operation.
+
+Compile-time constants are not present in the runtime variant pack. Replacing a constant requires a new graph identity and may require new plan compilation. Runtime parameters, by contrast, preserve graph structure and receive a host scalar binding at execution.
+
+## Runtime scalar tensors
+
+Use a regular device tensor when the value changes per execution or participates in broadcasting as data. It requires a runtime binding and follows normal tensor lifetime and layout rules.
+
+Canonical references: [`tensor_scalar`](/api/python/tensor-scalar) and [C++ `tensor_scalar`](/api/cpp/tensor-scalar).
+
+## Construct a constant FMA graph
+
+The published C++ sample constructs and validates a multiply-add graph whose scale and bias are embedded in graph identity. It is compiled against the current headers; kernel execution requires the newer backend recorded below.

+# Reshape, transpose, slice, and concatenate
+
+Choose whether a shape change is metadata-only or requires an executable graph operation, then preserve the resulting layout explicitly.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Complete [Build and extend a graph](/tutorials/first-graph) and review
+[logical shapes and physical strides](/concepts/layouts). For each
+operation, derive the expected output dimensions, strides, and values before
+building the graph. The standalone transpose, slice, and concatenate examples
+use the SM100 memory-bound path and require CUDA 13.1 and cuDNN 9.22 or newer.
+
+## Choose an operation
+
+### Reshape
+
+`reshape` changes dimensions according to `reshape_mode`. A reshape is view-like only when the new dimensions and strides describe the same storage; other modes can materialize or infer a supported layout.
+
+### Transpose
+
+`transpose` permutes logical axes, and its output dimensions and strides follow
+the permutation. A framework transpose can be a metadata-only view; the Graph
+operation shown below binds a separate output buffer.
+
+### Slice
+
+Slices use start, stop, and step values with half-open intervals. The output extent follows Python-style slice arithmetic in the Python IR. Non-unit or negative steps require explicit support from the selected operation path.
+
+### Concatenate
+
+Concatenate joins compatible inputs along one axis. Non-concatenated extents must match. In-place and out-of-place forms have different aliasing and lifetime constraints; bind every externally materialized input and output.

+# Diagnose graph failures
+
+Separate description errors, support failures, compilation failures, and runtime failures instead of retrying the complete build blindly.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Reproduce the failure with one graph, fixed inputs, and
+[`cudnn.pygraph` lifecycle stages](/how-to/explicit-lifecycle) exposed separately.
+Record the frontend, backend, CUDA, GPU, graph metadata, and first failing
+stage.
+
+## Validate the description
+
+Call `graph.validate()` first. Inspect dimensions, strides, data types, names, UIDs, virtual state, pass-by-value values, and inferred outputs. `ValueError` normally identifies an invalid Python IR relationship; C++ returns an `error_t` whose message names the failed frontend check.
+
+## Create the graph representation
+
+Call `graph.build_operation_graph()` separately. Failure here can indicate invalid backend descriptors, unavailable operation attributes, or a backend version that cannot represent the graph.
+
+## Inspect and select plans
+
+Call `graph.create_execution_plans()` and inspect `graph.plans`. A Python engine should decline only with a documented decline exception; another exception is an engine defect. For backend candidates, use engine and plan filters before compilation.
+
+## Check support and build
+
+`graph.check_support()` distinguishes a well-formed but unsupported graph. `graph.build_plans()` can still fail during kernel or plan compilation. Record the selected engine, knobs, behavior notes, numerical notes, workspace, backend version, GPU, and complete error.
+
+## Validate runtime bindings
+
+Provide every required non-virtual UID exactly once, enough workspace, compatible override arrays, and pointers valid until asynchronous work completes. Confirm the cuDNN handle uses the intended CUDA stream.
+
+## Enable logs
+
+```bash
+CUDNN_FRONTEND_LOG_INFO=1 CUDNN_FRONTEND_LOG_FILE=stdout <your command>
+```
+
+For numerical issues, compare one operation at a time in the same compute and output types. Synchronize before reading output or attributing a later asynchronous error to the wrong call.
+
+## Expected result
+
+The first failing lifecycle stage is isolated with its original status and
+complete graph context. Description errors are corrected before planning;
+unsupported graphs take only an explicit fallback; runtime failures are not
+misreported as plan-selection problems.

+# cuDNN Frontend
+
+cuDNN Frontend lets applications describe tensor computations as graphs and execute them on NVIDIA GPUs. You can use a deep learning framework, such as PyTorch, if it already provides the features and performance you need. Use cuDNN Frontend when you need finer control over the computation or features that the framework does not yet support.
+
+The repository provides a header-only C++ API, Python graph APIs, PyTorch integration, and optional open-source CUTLASS DSL kernels for selected attention, normalization, and GEMM workloads.
+
+## Choose a learning path
+
+### Python and PyTorch
+
+1. [Install the Python package](/getting-started/installation#python).
+2. [Run the Python quick start](/getting-started/quickstart).
+3. [Build your first `cudnn.Graph`](/tutorials/first-graph).
+4. [Integrate a reusable graph with PyTorch](/tutorials/pytorch-integration).
+5. Move to the [explicit `cudnn.pygraph` lifecycle](/how-to/explicit-lifecycle) only when you need routing, inspection, or plan control.
+
+### C++ application integration
+
+1. [Install or consume the header target](/getting-started/installation#c).
+2. [Run the C++ quick start](/getting-started/quickstart).
+3. Learn [runtime ownership and asynchronous execution](/concepts/runtime-resources).
+4. Use the [operation tutorials](/tutorials) and [deployment guides](/how-to).
+
+### Advanced kernels and deployment
+
+1. Learn [API layers and graph lifecycle](/concepts/api-layers).
+2. Choose [plans and autotune](/how-to/plan-selection).
+3. Add [dynamic shapes](/how-to/dynamic-shapes), [serialization](/how-to/deployment), or [CUDA Graphs](/how-to/cuda-graphs).
+4. Evaluate [low-precision formats](/how-to/low-precision) and [open-source engines](/optional-kernels/oss-engines) against the [compatibility matrix](/getting-started/compatibility).
+
+## Interfaces
+
+| Interface | Use it for |
+| --- | --- |
+| `cudnn.Graph` | Python-first PyTorch integration with automatic lifecycle, output allocation, and workspace ownership |
+| `cudnn.pygraph` | Explicit Python IR, inspection, custom routing, and lifecycle control |
+| `cudnn_frontend::graph::Graph` | Header-only C++ integration with explicit resources and complete Graph API control |
+| `cudnn.graph`, `cudnn.jit`, `graph_cache` | Shape-specialized Python graph construction and caching |
+| `cudnn.ops` | PyTorch custom operators supplied by this package |
+| OSS and experimental packages | Architecture-specific fused kernels and convenience operators with narrower stability guarantees |
+
+The documentation targets commit `0a07d4ee28f8ae2f2106bb766b1878cc732ee80c`. Feature availability still depends on the installed cuDNN backend, CUDA runtime, GPU architecture, shape, layout, data type, and engine.
+
+## Find exact contracts
+
+- [Tutorials](/tutorials) teach complete workflows.
+- [How-to guides](/how-to) solve focused integration tasks.
+- [Concepts](/concepts) explain the model and constraints.
+- [API reference](/api) is the alphabetical contract dictionary.
+- [Sample catalog](/verified-samples/catalog) publishes every executable example and its verification status.
+- [Verification record](/verification) identifies the environment, results, and limits behind documentation claims.

+- [Select an OSS engine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/main/docs/reference/oss-engines.md): Choose an OSS heuristic or direct kernel entry point.

+# OSS block-sparse attention contract
+
+Use `cudnn.BSA` when the attention pattern is already expressed as fixed-size query-to-key block metadata and the workload satisfies one of the architecture-specific CUTLASS DSL paths.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Install the `cutedsl` extra, use an architecture listed below, and prepare a
+dense attention reference plus valid INT32 block metadata. Validate every
+active block index and per-row count before invoking the wrapper.
+
+## Install and import
+
+Install the `cutedsl` extra from the same frontend checkout. `cudnn.BSA` is a lazy namespace; accessing it imports optional CUDA Python, PyTorch, and CUTLASS DSL dependencies. Import failure does not mean the cuDNN Graph API is unavailable.
+
+## block_sparse_attention_forward
+
+`cudnn.block_sparse_attention_forward(q_tensor, k_tensor, v_tensor, q2k_block_index, block_sparse_num=None, block_sizes=None, q2k_block_nums=None, *, sparse_block_size=None, allow_empty_block_nums=False, softmax_scale=None, pack_gqa=None, layout="bhsd", kv_splits=1, use_clc=None)` returns a tuple-like mapping with `o_tensor` and `lse_tensor`.
+
+The inputs use BHSD by default. `layout="bshd"` selects BSHD. Q, K, and V must be CUDA FP16 or BF16 tensors with a contiguous head dimension and compatible batch, head, and sequence dimensions. `softmax_scale=None` uses `1 / sqrt(D_qk)`.
+
+`q2k_block_index` is an INT32 tensor whose active prefix lists physical KV-block indices for each query block. Supply either one fixed `block_sparse_num` or an INT32 `q2k_block_nums` tensor with the per-row active counts. `block_sizes` optionally describes valid tokens in physical KV blocks. Active indices must be in range; duplicate indices are not combined for the caller.
+
+The forward support matrix is:
+
+| GPU | Sparse block | Q/K/V dtype | QK and V dimensions | Heads |
+| --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- |
+| SM90 | 64 | FP16 or BF16 | 64, 96, or 128 | MHA, GQA, MQA |
+| SM100/SM110 | 128 | FP16 or BF16 | matching 64, 96, or 128 | MHA, GQA, MQA |
+| SM100/SM110 | 64, explicitly selected | BF16 | QK=V=128 | MHA only |
+| SM120 | 64 | FP16 or BF16 | QK=V=128 | MHA, GQA, MQA |
+
+SM90 requires `S_q` to be a multiple of 64. The SM100/SM110 block-128 fixed count must be even and at least two. `pack_gqa` applies only to that block-128 path. Integer `kv_splits` is supported by SM90 and the explicit SM100/SM110 block-64 path; `kv_splits="auto"` and `use_clc` are specific to the latter.
+
+## block_sparse_attention_fp8_forward
+
+The Sage FP8 wrapper is forward-only. It accepts contiguous BF16 Q, K, and V in BHSD layout, quantizes them internally to E4M3, and returns one BF16 `o_tensor`; it does not return LSE and has no corresponding backward API. Inputs must use MHA with `D=128` and matching batch, head, and sequence metadata.
+
+SM90, SM100/SM103, and SM120 support sparse block size 64 or 128 with architecture-specific metadata rules. SM90 requires both sequence lengths to be multiples of the chosen block size and accepts only fixed counts. SM100/SM103 block 64 also requires aligned sequence lengths and fixed counts; its split-KV choice is internal. The native SM100/SM103 block-128 path accepts physical tails, empty variable-count rows, rank-1 through rank-3 `block_sizes`, and explicit `kv_splits` from 1 through 256. SM120 accepts sequence tails, fixed or per-query-block counts, and rank-1 through rank-3 block sizes without split-KV.
+
+Outputs are approximate and need not be bitwise identical across block sizes or architectures. The wrapper requires CuTe DSL 4.6.1 or later; the SM90 block-128 path requires 4.6.2 or later.
+
+## block_sparse_attention_backward
+
+`cudnn.block_sparse_attention_backward(do_tensor, q_tensor, k_tensor, v_tensor, o_tensor, lse_tensor, q2k_block_index, block_sparse_num=None, block_sizes=None, q2k_block_nums=None, *, softmax_scale=None, dq_tensor=None, dk_tensor=None, dv_tensor=None, bucket_size_blocks=None, sparse_block_size=None, layout="bhsd")` returns `dq_tensor`, `dk_tensor`, and `dv_tensor`.
+
+Backward must receive the forward output, natural-log LSE, sparse metadata, layout, scale, and block-size choice from the matching forward pass. Optional gradient outputs allow caller-owned storage. The current backward paths require BF16, equal QK/V dimensions, and MHA:
+
+| GPU | Sparse block | Head dimension |
+| --- | ---: | ---: |
+| SM90 | 64 | 128 |
+| SM100/SM110 | 64 | 128 |
+| SM100/SM110 | 128 | 64 or 128 |
+
+SM120 backward is not implemented. The SM100/SM110 block-128 path does not consume `block_sizes`; pass `None` and use full physical KV blocks.
+
+## Reuse compiled kernels
+
+The wrapper caches compiled specializations. Treat device, architecture, dtype, complete shape and stride metadata, sparse block size, tiling choices, and relevant flags as part of the specialization identity. Reuse input and output buffers only when their metadata still matches the compiled contract.
+
+Current implementation: [public wrapper and validation](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/0a07d4ee28f8ae2f2106bb766b1878cc732ee80c/python/cudnn/block_sparse_attention/api.py#L148).
+
+## Expected result
+
+Forward returns output and natural-log LSE for the selected sparse pattern;
+supported backward paths reproduce the corresponding dense masked gradients.
+This page records the source contract but does not publish a documentation-owned
+executable sample, so verify both results on the target architecture.

+# OSS DeepSeek sparse-attention contract
+
+Use `cudnn.DSA` for the score, selection, recomputation, and backward stages used by DeepSeek-style sparse attention. The namespace contains independent wrappers; it is not one end-to-end operator and does not infer routing metadata between stages.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Install the `cutedsl` extra, select one DSA stage, and prepare every intermediate
+that stage consumes. Record the deployed architecture, shape, dtype, layout,
+top-k convention, and softmax scale in the specialization key.
+
+## DSA namespace
+
+`cudnn.DSA` is a lazy namespace object that exports the classes and wrappers listed below. Importing it loads optional CUTLASS DSL dependencies; it does not compile a kernel until a class or wrapper receives tensors.
+
+## Choose a stage
+
+| Public wrapper | Purpose | Principal outputs | Current architecture |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| `sparse_attention_backward_wrapper` | Backpropagate sparse attention | `dq`, `dkv`, `d_sink` | SM90 or SM100 |
+| `indexer_forward_wrapper` | Compute dense indexer scores | `scores` | SM100+ |
+| `indexer_top_k_wrapper` | Select local top-k entries | `indices`, optional `values` | SM90+ |
+| `local_to_global_wrapper` | Convert local top-k indices | global `indices` | Same device as indices |
+| `compactify_wrapper` | Pack valid indices | `indices`, `topk_length` | Same device as indices |
+| `sparse_indexer_score_recompute_wrapper` | Recompute selected indexer scores | `predict` | SM90 or SM100 |
+| `sparse_attn_score_recompute_wrapper` | Recompute selected attention scores | `target` | SM90 or SM100 |
+| `dense_indexer_score_recompute_wrapper` | Recompute full-KV indexer scores | scores and denominator | SM90 or SM100 |
+| `dense_attn_score_recompute_wrapper` | Recompute full-KV attention scores | scores and denominator | SM90 or SM100 |
+| `indexer_backward_wrapper` | Backpropagate selected indexer scores | index-Q, weights, and index-K gradients | SM90 or SM100 |
+| `dense_indexer_backward_wrapper` | Backpropagate the dense indexer path | index-Q, weights, and index-K gradients | SM90 or SM100 |
+
+## indexer_forward_wrapper
+
+Pass CUDA `q`, `k`, and `w` tensors plus `ratio`, optional `qhead_per_kv_head`, block sizes, stages, and `sm_scale`. The fixed-shape path requires head dimension 128 and supports `qhead_per_kv_head` values 32 or 64. The wrapper also accepts THD metadata through `cu_seqlens_q`, `cu_seqlens_k`, maximum sequence lengths, and optional query causal offsets.
+
+The returned score tensor includes TMA padding on the physical KV extent. Use the documented logical sequence length when feeding top-k; do not interpret padded columns as valid keys.
+
+## indexer_top_k_wrapper
+
+Pass a two-dimensional score view, per-row valid sequence lengths, `top_k`, and optional `next_n`. `top_k` must be positive and no greater than 2048. `return_val=False` omits values. The indices are local to the row's current KV range unless converted with `local_to_global_wrapper`.
+
+## Score recomputation
+
+Sparse recomputation consumes top-k indices and optionally `topk_length`. `topk_indices_global` must match the index representation produced by the preceding stage. Dense recomputation accepts optional THD sequence metadata. Indexer recomputation also consumes learned weights; attention recomputation consumes LSE and the same softmax scale used by attention forward.
+
+Output tensors are FP32 score data. Caller-provided `out` and denominator buffers must have the exact shape, dtype, device, and contiguous dimension required by the selected implementation.
+
+## Backward stages
+
+`sparse_attention_backward_wrapper` consumes Q, combined KV, forward output, upstream gradient, natural-log LSE, sink values, and selected indices. Its FlashMLA-shaped SM90 path supports head dimensions 512 and 576; other shapes are checked by the current implementation. Preserve `softmax_scale` and `topk_length` from forward.
+
+`indexer_backward_wrapper` runs three stages and accumulates into caller-provided or allocated gradient tensors. `dense_indexer_backward_wrapper` additionally accepts dense-attention L1 norm, indexer LSE, THD metadata, and causal offsets. Both accept a scalar FP32 `grad_loss` and optional `loss_coeff`.
+
+## Class APIs
+
+Kernel-backed stages have corresponding classes such as `IndexerForward`, `IndexerTopK`, `SparseAttentionBackward`, or `DenseIndexerBackward`. Construct the class with representative sample tensors to compile a specialization, then call `execute` with tensors of the same metadata. `local_to_global_wrapper` and `compactify_wrapper` are utility wrappers without public class counterparts. Prefer wrappers for one-off use and classes when the caller owns cache lifetime and repeated execution.
+
+Current exports: [DSA namespace](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/0a07d4ee28f8ae2f2106bb766b1878cc732ee80c/python/cudnn/deepseek_sparse_attention/__init__.py#L52).
+
+## Expected result
+
+The selected stage writes outputs with the documented shape and precision and
+matches an independently composed dense or sparse reference. No end-to-end DSA
+sample is published here; source-level wrapper inventory does not establish
+runtime support for an untested combination.

+# OSS dense GEMM fusion contracts
+
+Use the optional dense GEMM wrappers for Blackwell block-scaled matrix products whose epilogue exactly matches one of the exported fusions. These wrappers call CUTLASS DSL kernels directly and do not inherit cuDNN Graph fallback behavior.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Install the `cutedsl` extra, use SM100 or newer, and establish a dense
+higher-precision reference. Derive the scale-factor layout with the selected
+wrapper's utilities instead of treating it as an ordinary matrix.
+
+## Prepare block-scaled operands
+
+All five families require an SM100+ CUDA device, but they do not share one dtype contract. Amax, sReLU, and dsReLU are block-scaled paths. SwiGLU selects a dense path when SFA/SFB are absent and a block-scaled path when both are present. Projection+RoPE accepts fixed BF16 inputs and produces MXFP8 outputs. For block-scaled calls, scale tensors must use the layout computed for `sf_vec_size`, the MMA tile, and operand dimensions; they are not ordinary dense `[M, K]` tensors.
+
+Treat `mma_tiler_mn`, `cluster_shape_mn`, scale vector size, major-order flags, output dtype, and optional two-CTA scheduling as compilation inputs. The common cluster rule is positive dimensions no greater than four with total cluster size no greater than 16; individual kernels can impose stricter combinations.
+
+## gemm_amax_wrapper_sm100
+
+`cudnn.gemm_amax_wrapper_sm100` computes a block-scaled GEMM and returns the matrix output plus its absolute maximum. Supply A, B, SFA, and SFB with compatible shapes. Choose output dtype and layout through the wrapper options. The amax result is FP32 and must not be interpreted as a per-row scale.
+
+Signature: `gemm_amax_wrapper_sm100(a_tensor, b_tensor, sfa_tensor, sfb_tensor, c_major="n", c_dtype=torch.float32, acc_dtype=torch.float32, mma_tiler_mn=(128, 128), cluster_shape_mn=(1, 1), sf_vec_size=32, stream=None)`. A and B are rank-3 `[M, K, L]` and `[N, K, L]` with the same FP4 or FP8 dtype. `sf_vec_size` is 16 or 32 subject to the input/scale dtype combination. Accumulation is FP32; C can be FP32, FP16, BF16, FP8, or compatible FP4. Cluster dimensions must be powers of two in `{1, 2, 4}`. The current validator rejects an M tile of 256 and several additional launch combinations.
+
+### GemmAmaxSm100
+
+Use `cudnn.GemmAmaxSm100` when outputs are preallocated. Its constructor compiles from representative inputs and its `execute` method writes C and amax on the selected stream.
+
+## gemm_srelu_wrapper_sm100
+
+`cudnn.gemm_srelu_wrapper_sm100` applies ReLU after the GEMM and may quantize the activated result. `prob_tensor` is a required FP32 `[M, 1, L]` input; `norm_const_tensor` is optional. The result mapping contains `c_tensor`, `d_tensor`, and optional `sfd_tensor` or `amax_tensor`.
+
+Signature: `gemm_srelu_wrapper_sm100(a_tensor, b_tensor, sfa_tensor, sfb_tensor, prob_tensor, alpha=1.0, c_major="n", c_dtype=torch.bfloat16, d_dtype=torch.bfloat16, acc_dtype=torch.float32, mma_tiler_mn=(256, 256), cluster_shape_mn=None, norm_const_tensor=None, sf_vec_size=16, vector_f32=False, stream=None)`. A and B use the same FP4 or FP8 dtype; SFA and SFB use the same E8M0 or E4M3 scale dtype. FP8 D requires both an allocated SFD and `norm_const_tensor`; the wrapper allocates SFD. FP4 input with floating D produces FP32 amax. C and D share the selected major order.
+
+### GemmSreluSm100
+
+`cudnn.GemmSreluSm100` is the caller-allocation class form.
+
+## gemm_dsrelu_wrapper_sm100
+
+`cudnn.gemm_dsrelu_wrapper_sm100` implements the backward derivative for the ReLU fusion. It consumes required A, B, forward C, SFA, SFB, and FP32 probability tensors. It returns `d_tensor`, FP32 `dprob_tensor`, and optional `sfd_tensor` or `amax_tensor`.
+
+Signature: `gemm_dsrelu_wrapper_sm100(a_tensor, b_tensor, c_tensor, sfa_tensor, sfb_tensor, prob_tensor, alpha=1.0, d_major="n", d_dtype=torch.bfloat16, acc_dtype=torch.float32, mma_tiler_mn=(256, 256), cluster_shape_mn=None, norm_const_tensor=None, sf_vec_size=16, vector_f32=False, stream=None)`. C must be floating FP16, BF16, or FP32. D can additionally be FP8, which requires the wrapper-created SFD and an explicit normalization constant. Use the same shape, scale-vector size, alpha, and probability data as forward.
+
+### GemmDsreluSm100
+
+`cudnn.GemmDsreluSm100` is not interchangeable with the forward class: its input roles, output gradients, and epilogue validation are different.
+
+## gemm_swiglu_wrapper_sm100
+
+`cudnn.gemm_swiglu_wrapper_sm100` splits the GEMM output into gate and value halves and applies a SwiGLU epilogue. The GEMM N dimension must therefore be compatible with an even split. It returns full-width `ab12_tensor`, half-width `c_tensor`, and optional `sfc_tensor` or `amax_tensor`.
+
+Signature: `gemm_swiglu_wrapper_sm100(a_tensor, b_tensor, alpha=1.0, c_major="n", ab12_dtype=torch.float32, c_dtype=torch.float16, acc_dtype=torch.float32, mma_tiler_mn=(128, 128), cluster_shape_mn=None, sfa_tensor=None, sfb_tensor=None, norm_const_tensor=None, sf_vec_size=16, vector_f32=False, ab12_stages=4, stream=None)`. Omit both scale tensors for the dense path, which accepts matching FP16, BF16, FP32, or FP8 A/B. Supply both for the block-scaled FP4/FP8 path. FP8 C requires SFC and `norm_const_tensor`; FP4 input with BF16 C produces amax. Layouts require 16-byte alignment, and the block-scaled path aligns M and N to its MMA tile.
+
+### GemmSwigluSm100
+
+`cudnn.GemmSwigluSm100` exposes explicit compile and execute phases with caller-provided C, D, scale, and amax buffers.
+
+## gemm_proj_rope_mxfp8_wrapper_sm100
+
+`cudnn.gemm_proj_rope_mxfp8_wrapper_sm100` fuses projection GEMM, per-head RoPE, and dual-direction MXFP8 quantization. It requires projection and frequency metadata that agree on token count, head count, head dimension, and rotated dimension. Its result contains the row- and column-oriented quantized Q representations and corresponding scale factors.
+
+Signature: `gemm_proj_rope_mxfp8_wrapper_sm100(x, w, cos, sin, w_out_in=False, stream=None)`. X is BF16 `[tokens, Q_LORA]`. W is BF16 `[Q_LORA, heads * 192]`, or its transpose when `w_out_in=True`. Cos and sin are BF16 `[tokens, 64]`. Tokens must be a multiple of 128. Outputs are E4M3 `[tokens, heads, 192]` data plus E8M0 scales in rowwise `[tokens, heads, 6]` and columnwise `[tokens / 32, heads, 192]` layouts.
+
+This fusion has a narrower contract than calling Graph matmul, RoPE, and block scaling separately. Use the composed Graph path when the model needs a different RoPE layout, dtype, or materialized intermediate.
+
+### GemmProjRopeMxfp8Sm100
+
+`cudnn.GemmProjRopeMxfp8Sm100` owns the compiled specialization and accepts caller-provided projection, frequency, quantized output, and scale buffers at execution.
+
+## Select wrapper or class form
+
+Wrappers allocate outputs and return a `TupleDict` that supports named and positional access. Class constructors accept sample tensors and compile a specialization; `execute` requires caller-owned outputs with identical metadata. Do not share one class instance across devices or incompatible streams unless its source contract explicitly permits it.
+
+Current sources: [`gemm_amax`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/0a07d4ee28f8ae2f2106bb766b1878cc732ee80c/python/cudnn/gemm_amax/api.py#L18), [`gemm_srelu`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/0a07d4ee28f8ae2f2106bb766b1878cc732ee80c/python/cudnn/gemm_srelu/api.py#L32), [`gemm_dsrelu`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/0a07d4ee28f8ae2f2106bb766b1878cc732ee80c/python/cudnn/gemm_dsrelu/api.py#L32), [`gemm_swiglu`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/0a07d4ee28f8ae2f2106bb766b1878cc732ee80c/python/cudnn/gemm_swiglu/api.py#L49), and [`gemm_proj_rope_mxfp8`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/0a07d4ee28f8ae2f2106bb766b1878cc732ee80c/python/cudnn/gemm_proj_rope_mxfp8/api.py#L22).
+
+## Expected result
+
+A supported wrapper matches the dense reference within the tolerance selected
+for its quantization and epilogue, and class-form reuse preserves all
+specialization metadata. This page has no executable documentation sample, so
+run those checks before replacing a Graph fallback.

+# OSS discrete-weight grouped GEMM contracts
+
+Use discrete grouped GEMM when expert weights and scale factors are supplied as device pointer arrays rather than one contiguous expert tensor. The current checkout exports forward GLU and backward dGLU families for SM100+.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Install the `cutedsl` extra, use SM100 or newer, and build device pointer arrays
+whose pointed-to expert buffers remain alive through stream completion. Keep a
+per-expert dense reference and validated padded offsets.
+
+## Build pointer arrays
+
+`b_ptrs` and `sfb_ptrs` are CUDA tensors containing device addresses for each expert's B and SFB allocation. The pointed-to buffers must remain alive until the asynchronous kernel completes. Every expert must use the declared N, K, dtype, major order, and scale layout. Pointer-array storage itself must have the dtype and alignment expected by the wrapper.
+
+Use monotonic `padded_offsets` to map contiguous A rows to experts. `alpha` provides per-expert scaling. Cache identity includes the declared weight shape and dtype, but pointer values may change between compatible executions.
+
+## discrete_grouped_gemm_swiglu_wrapper_sm100
+
+`cudnn.discrete_grouped_gemm_swiglu_wrapper_sm100` computes pointer-based grouped GEMM followed by the selected GLU activation. Required inputs are A, B pointer array, SFA, SFB pointer array, padded offsets, alpha, N, and B dtype. Optional bias, normalization constant, probability, activation parameters, and scheduling affect the epilogue.
+
+The result includes the pre-activation C and GLU output D. Floating outputs may include amax; quantized outputs include row and column scale factors. The pre-activation N dimension must be compatible with the two GLU halves.
+
+### DiscreteGroupedGemmSwigluSm100
+
+The class form is `cudnn.DiscreteGroupedGemmSwigluSm100`.
+
+## discrete_grouped_gemm_dswiglu_wrapper_sm100
+
+`cudnn.discrete_grouped_gemm_dswiglu_wrapper_sm100` computes the pointer-based GLU backward fusion. It consumes A, B pointers, C, SFA, SFB pointers, offsets, alpha, beta, routing probability, and its gradient. Set `generate_dbias=True` only when the selected activation and layout support bias-gradient generation.
+
+Use the same `act_func`, linear offset, GeGLU alpha, clamp bounds, N, weight dtype, weight major order, and scale layout as forward. Results include row- and column-oriented gradient data plus optional scale, amax, probability-gradient, and bias-gradient tensors according to dtype and flags.
+
+### DiscreteGroupedGemmDswigluSm100
+
+The class form is `cudnn.DiscreteGroupedGemmDswigluSm100`.
+
+## Validate before launch
+
+Both wrappers require SM100+, FP32 accumulation, legal low-precision operand types, aligned dimensions, compatible scale-factor shapes, and a supported MMA tile and cluster. Device pointer arrays create no ownership: freeing one expert allocation before stream completion is a use-after-free.
+
+Current package exports: [discrete grouped GEMM namespace](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/blob/0a07d4ee28f8ae2f2106bb766b1878cc732ee80c/python/cudnn/discrete_grouped_gemm/__init__.py#L1).
+
+## Expected result
+
+Forward and backward outputs match the same expert boundaries and activation
+parameters as the dense reference, and changing compatible pointer values does
+not change specialization identity. No executable documentation sample is
+published, so pointer lifetime and numerical checks remain deployment gates.

+# Optional OSS engine contracts
+
+Use optional open-source kernels only when their exported wrapper, dependencies, architecture, layout, and fallback contract match the workload.
+
+## Before you begin
+
+Install the optional packages from the same frontend checkout and identify the
+target GPU architecture. Establish a cuDNN Graph or framework reference before
+replacing it with an OSS wrapper.
+
+## Install optional dependencies
+
+Install the `cutedsl` extra to obtain the pinned CUTLASS DSL package, CUDA Python, PyTorch, TVM FFI, and DLPack extension declared by this checkout. Keep the frontend, optional packages, CUDA runtime, and GPU architecture compatible.
+
+## Choose an entry point
+
+- `heur_mode.OPENSOURCE` lets the Graph backend consider registered OSS slots.
+- Top-level optional exports provide fused SM100 GEMM, grouped GEMM, SDPA D=256, and RMSNorm kernels.
+- `cudnn.BSA`, `cudnn.DSA`, and `cudnn.NSA` expose sparse-attention families.
+- `cudnn.experimental.ops` provides PyTorch convenience operators with explicit experimental status.
+
+The legacy OSS guide set covered these distinct families. Keep each item in the
+inventory even when several wrappers share an implementation or dependency:
+
+- Sparse attention: [BSA](/optional-kernels/oss-block-sparse-attention), [DSA](/optional-kernels/oss-deepseek-sparse-attention), and [NSA](/optional-kernels/oss-native-sparse-attention).
+- Attention: [SDPA forward and backward with head dimension 256](/optional-kernels/oss-sdpa-d256).
+- [Dense fused GEMM](/optional-kernels/oss-dense-gemm): amax, dReLU, projection plus RoPE MXFP8, ReLU, and SwiGLU variants.
+- [Grouped GEMM](/optional-kernels/oss-grouped-gemm): dGLU, dReLU, dSwiGLU, GLU, GLU plus Hadamard, quantized, ReLU, SwiGLU, and weight-gradient variants.
+- [Discrete grouped GEMM](/optional-kernels/oss-discrete-grouped-gemm): SwiGLU and dSwiGLU variants.
+- [Normalization](/optional-kernels/oss-normalization): RMSNorm plus randomized Hadamard transform and amax. The former RMSNorm+SiLU package is absent from the current checkout.
+
+## Validate support before execution
+
+Inspect the package `__all__`, wrapper validation, test shapes, and architecture checks. Optional imports are lazy and raise an installation hint when dependencies are absent. Do not document implementation helpers that are not exported, and do not assume every exported wrapper supports the same stream or allocation contract.
+
+## Preserve fallback boundaries
+
+For Graph planning, keep a cuDNN backend heuristic entry when fallback is desired. Direct wrapper calls have no automatic Graph fallback unless their source contract implements one.
+
+## Expected result
+
+An imported wrapper accepts the exact deployed shape, dtype, layout, and
+architecture and matches the reference result. Unsupported optional imports or
+kernel contracts leave the ordinary Graph path available as an explicit
+fallback; direct wrapper calls do not acquire one automatically.
